title: An Adaptive Machine Learning Algorithm for the Resource-Constrained Classification Problem
authors: Danit Abukasis Shifman, Izack Cohen, Kejun Huang, Xiaochen Xian, Gonen Singer
conclusions: Proposes AdaCSL-WRC, a decision-tree cost-sensitive learning algorithm that folds a hard per-class RESOURCE CONSTRAINT (max number of instances allowed to be classified positive, e.g. limited COVID test kits) into training by iteratively incrementing the false-positive misclassification cost c(0,1) each round.

At each iteration a 'classifier-dependent threshold' (Eq. 16, Algorithm 1) is computed that forces the TRAINING set's positive-classification count to exactly equal the projected budget B(1); the loop stops once the classifier's own cost-optimal threshold tau already satisfies the constraint without needing the forced threshold.

The final chosen model M* is then applied to the TEST set using its ordinary cost-sensitive decision rule (Eq. 4/5) -- there is no hard threshold re-enforcement at test time, so the resource constraint is approximated via adapted costs rather than guaranteed exactly on held-out data.

On a Kaggle direct-marketing dataset (binary, resource constraint = 25-75% of positive-campaign count), AdaCSL-WRC beats a plain decision tree and a naive cost-sensitive decision tree + post-hoc allocation baseline on cost, precision and accuracy, with significance (p<0.05) concentrated in harder/scarcer-resource regimes.
Theoretical result: under full resource utilization, minimizing cost is equivalent to maximizing accuracy and precision simultaneously (Section 3.1).
Binary classification only, single global constraint (no local/group sub-caps), decision-tree-specific (relies on decision trees' discrete leaf-probability subsets for the threshold construction).
our_use: main.tex:194 -- "Other work in this line folds the budget into learning via adaptive cost-sensitive weights \citep{shifman2023adaptive} or predict-and-optimize ranking under stochastic capacity \citep{vanderschueren2024perspective}, steering expected costs rather than enforcing a hard count" -- cited as a training-time (not post-hoc) method that bakes the resource budget into learning via adaptively tuned misclassification costs, contrasted with TraLO's hard-count Lagrangian mechanism.
